steps.title: France and Spain
steps.body: Carignan was once France's most planted grape, especially in the Languedoc, where it made cheap, high-yield table wine. EU vine-pull schemes from the 1980s cut plantings dramatically. In Spain it grows in Priorat, Montsant, Empordà and Rioja. In Italy, Sardinia's Carignano del Sulcis is its stronghold.

steps.title: Blends
steps.body: In the Languedoc and Roussillon, Carignan blends with Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre, adding acidity and colour. In Priorat, it partners Garnacha. In Rioja, as Mazuelo, it's a minor partner to Tempranillo, adding acidity and colour. Carbonic maceration, the Beaujolais method, is sometimes used to soften it.

steps.prompt: Why were many Languedoc Carignan vineyards pulled out from the 1980s?
options: EU schemes to reduce wine surplus
steps.explanation: Vine-pull schemes targeted high-yield, low-value vineyards, many planted with Carignan.

steps.body: Look for Vieilles Vignes, old vines, on Languedoc Carignan labels. Old-vine Carignan is far more concentrated than the bulk wine that gave it a poor reputation.

steps.prompt: Which grapes does Carignan often blend with?
steps.explanation: Riesling isn't a Mediterranean blending partner.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Carignan was France's most planted grape; plantings fell sharply
It blends with Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre
